danish.title: Anden bog (1805) — Kapitel 14
paragraphs: Den 1. november havde Kutuzov gennem en spion fået nyheder om, at den hær, han førte, befandt sig i en næsten håbløs stilling. Spionen rapporterede, at franskmændene efter at have krydset broen ved Wien rykkede frem med enorme styrker mod Kutuzovs forbindelseslinje med de tropper, der var på vej fra Rusland. Hvis Kutuzov besluttede sig for at blive i Krems, ville Napoleons hær på hundrede og halvtreds tusind mand fuldstændig afskære ham og omringe hans udmattede hær på fyrre tusind, og han ville befinde sig i samme stilling som Mack ved Ulm. Hvis Kutuzov besluttede at opgive vejen, der forbandt ham med de tropper, der var på vej fra Rusland, ville han måtte marchere uden vej ind i ukendte dele af de bøhmiske bjerge, kæmpe mod overlegne fjendtlige styrker og opgive ethvert håb om at forene sig med Buxhöwden. Hvis Kutuzov besluttede at trække sig tilbage ad vejen fra Krems til Olmütz for at forene sig med tropperne fra Rusland, risikerede han at blive overhalet på den vej af franskmændene, der havde krydset Wien-broen, og tynget af sit bagage og train at måtte acceptere kamp under marchen mod en fjende, der var tre gange så stærk og som ville omringe ham fra to sider.
Kutuzov valgte den sidstnævnte mulighed.

Franskmændene, rapporterede spionen, havde efter at have krydset Wien-broen rykket frem i ilmarcher mod Znaim, der lå hundrede og seks kilometer borte på Kutuzovs tilbagetogsrute. Hvis han nåede Znaim før franskmændene, var der godt håb om at redde hæren; at lade franskmændene nå Znaim først betød at udsætte hele hans hær for en vanære som den ved Ulm eller ligefrem fuldstændig tilintetgørelse. Men at nå Znaim før franskmændene med hele sin hær var umuligt. Vejen for franskmændene fra Wien til Znaim var kortere og bedre end vejen for russerne fra Krems til Znaim.

Om natten, da han modtog nyheden, sendte Kutuzov Bagrations fortrop — fire tusind mand stærk — til højre over bakkerne fra Krems-Znaim-vejen til Wien-Znaim-vejen. Bagration skulle gennemføre denne march uden hvil og gøre holdt med front mod Wien og Znaim bag sig, og hvis det lykkedes ham at nå frem før franskmændene, skulle han forsinke dem så længe som muligt. Kutuzov selv tog med hele sit train vejen til Znaim.

Efter at have tilbagelagt halvtreds kilometer den stormfulde nat over vejløse bakker med sine sultne soldater i dårligt fodtøj og efter at have mistet en tredjedel af sine folk som efternølere undervejs, nåede Bagration Wien-Znaim-vejen ved Hollabrünn nogle timer før franskmændene, der nærmede sig Hollabrünn fra Wien. Kutuzov med sit train havde stadig flere dages march, før han kunne nå Znaim. Derfor måtte Bagration med sine fire tusind sultne, udmattede mænd holde hele den fjendtlige hær, der stødte på ham ved Hollabrünn, tilbage i dagevis, hvilket tydeligt var umuligt. Men et lune af skæbnen gjorde det umulige muligt. Succesen med det trick, der havde lagt Wien-broen i franskmændenes hænder uden kamp, fik Murat til at forsøge at narre Kutuzov på lignende vis. Da han stødte på Bagrations svage deling på Znaim-vejen, antog han, at det var hele Kutuzovs hær. For at kunne knuse den fuldstændig afventede han ankomsten af resten af de tropper, der var på vej fra Wien, og tilbød med dette formål en tre dages våbenhvile på betingelse af, at begge hære forblev på deres positioner uden at rykke sig. Murat erklærede, at fredsforhandlinger allerede var i gang, og at han derfor tilbød denne våbenhvile for at undgå unødvendig blodsudgydelse. Grev Nostitz, den østrigske general der besatte forposterne, troede på Murats udsending og trak sig tilbage og efterlod Bagrations division ubeskyttet. En anden udsending red til den russiske linje for at meddele fredsforhandlingerne og tilbyde den russiske hær tre dages våbenhvile. Bagration svarede, at han ikke var bemyndiget til hverken at acceptere eller afvise en våbenhvile, og sendte sin adjutant til Kutuzov for at rapportere det tilbud, han havde modtaget.

En våbenhvile var Kutuzovs eneste chance for at vinde tid, give Bagrations udmattede tropper lidt hvile og lade transporten og de tunge konvojer (hvis bevægelser var skjult for franskmændene) rykke blot én etape nærmere Znaim. Tilbuddet om våbenhvile gav den eneste og ganske uventede chance for at redde hæren. Da han modtog nyheden, sendte han straks generaladjutant Wintzingerode, der var i hans følge, til fjendtlig lejr. Wintzingerode skulle ikke blot acceptere våbenhvilen, men også tilbyde kapitulationsbetingelser, og i mellemtiden sendte Kutuzov sine adjutanter tilbage for at skynde mest muligt på bagagetrainets bevægelser langs Krems-Znaim-vejen. Bagrations udmattede og sultne deling, der alene dækkede denne bevægelse af transporten og hele hæren, måtte forblive stationær stående over for en fjende, der var otte gange så stærk.

Kutuzovs forventning om, at kapitulationsforslaget (som på ingen måde var bindende) kunne give tid til, at en del af transporten kom forbi, og at Murats fejltagelse meget snart ville blive opdaget, viste sig at holde stik. Så snart Bonaparte (der var i Schönbrunn, seksogtyve kilometer fra Hollabrünn) modtog Murats depeche med forslaget om våbenhvile og kapitulation, gennemskuede han et kneb og skrev følgende brev til Murat:
Schönbrunn, den 25. brumaire 1805,
klokken otte om morgenen
Til FYRST MURAT,

Jeg kan ikke finde ord til at udtrykke min mishag. De kommanderer kun min fortrop og har ingen ret til at aftale en våbenstilstand uden min ordre. De får mig til at miste frugterne af et felttog. Bryd våbenstilstanden øjeblikkeligt og march mod fjenden. Meddel ham, at den general, der underskrev den kapitulation, ikke havde ret til at gøre det, og at ingen andre end den russiske kejser har den ret.

Hvis den russiske kejser imidlertid ratificerer den konvention, vil jeg ratificere den; men det er kun et trick. March videre, tilintetgør den russiske hær... De er i en position til at beslaglægge dens bagage og artilleri.

Den russiske kejsers adjutant er en bedrager. Officerer er intet, når de ikke har fuldmagt; denne havde ingen... Østrigerne lod sig narre ved Wien-broen, De lader Dem narre af en adjutant hos kejseren.
NAPOLEON

Bonapartes adjutant red i fuld galop med dette truende brev til Murat. Bonaparte selv, der ikke stolede på sine generaler, rykkede med hele Garden mod slagmarken af frygt for at lade et sikkert bytte slippe, og Bagrations fire tusind mand tændte muntert lejrbål, tørrede og varmede sig, kogte deres grød for første gang i tre dage, og ikke én af dem vidste eller anede, hvad der ventede dem.

english.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: On November 1st, Kutúzov had received intelligence from a spy that the army he commanded was in a nearly hopeless situation. The spy reported that the French, having crossed the bridge at Vienna, were advancing in massive force toward Kutúzov's line of communication with the reinforcements arriving from Russia. If Kutúzov chose to remain at Krems, Napoleon's army of a hundred and fifty thousand men would completely cut him off and surround his exhausted force of forty thousand—and he would find himself in the same position as Mack at Ulm. If he chose to abandon the road connecting him with the approaching Russian reinforcements, he would have to march without roads into the unknown terrain of the Bohemian mountains, fighting off a superior enemy while giving up all hope of linking up with Buxhöwden. If he chose to retreat along the road from Krems to Olmütz to join the incoming Russian troops, he risked being overtaken on that road by the French who had crossed the Vienna bridge—and burdened by his baggage and supply trains, he would have to fight on the march against an enemy three times his strength attacking from two directions.
Kutúzov chose this last option.

The French, according to the spy, had crossed the Vienna bridge and were making forced marches toward Znaim, which lay sixty-six miles along Kutúzov's line of retreat. If he reached Znaim before the French, there was real hope of saving the army. If the French got there first, the entire army faced either the kind of humiliation Mack had suffered at Ulm, or total annihilation. But it was impossible for Kutúzov to reach Znaim ahead of the French with his whole army. The French road from Vienna to Znaim was shorter and better than the Russian road from Krems to Znaim.

The night he received this intelligence, Kutúzov sent Bagratión's advance guard—four thousand men—to the right, across the hills from the Krems-Znaim road to the Vienna-Znaim road. Bagratión was to make this march without stopping to rest and to take up a position facing Vienna with Znaim at his back. If he managed to get there ahead of the French, he was to hold them off for as long as possible. Kutúzov himself, with the rest of the army and all the supply trains, took the road to Znaim.

Marching thirty miles through a stormy night across trackless hills, with hungry, poorly shod soldiers, and losing a third of his men as stragglers along the way, Bagratión reached the Vienna-Znaim road at Hollabrünn a few hours ahead of the French approaching from Vienna. Kutúzov and his supply trains still had several days of marching before they could reach Znaim. So Bagratión, with his four thousand hungry, exhausted men, would have to hold off the entire enemy army for days at Hollabrünn—which was clearly impossible. But a twist of fate made the impossible possible. The success of the trick that had handed the Vienna bridge to the French without a fight led Murat to try deceiving Kutúzov in the same way. When Murat encountered Bagratión's small detachment on the Znaim road, he mistook it for Kutúzov's entire army. To ensure he could crush it completely, he waited for the rest of his troops still coming from Vienna, and in the meantime offered a three-day truce on the condition that both armies hold their positions without moving. Murat declared that peace negotiations were already underway, and that he was therefore proposing the truce to avoid unnecessary bloodshed. Count Nostitz, the Austrian general commanding the forward positions, believed Murat's envoy and pulled back, leaving Bagratión's division exposed. Another envoy rode to the Russian lines to announce the peace talks and offer the Russian army a three-day truce. Bagratión replied that he had no authority to accept or reject a truce and sent his adjutant to Kutúzov to report the offer.

A truce was Kutúzov's only chance to buy time, give Bagratión's worn-out troops some rest, and let the baggage and heavy supply trains—whose movements were hidden from the French—advance at least one more stage toward Znaim. The truce offer was the only chance, and a completely unexpected one, of saving the army. As soon as he received the news, Kutúzov immediately dispatched Adjutant General Wintzingerode to the enemy camp. Wintzingerode was not merely to agree to the truce but also to propose terms of surrender—and meanwhile, Kutúzov sent his adjutants racing back to push the movement of the entire army's baggage trains along the Krems-Znaim road as fast as possible. Bagratión's exhausted and hungry detachment, which alone was covering the movement of the supply trains and the whole army, had to remain in place facing an enemy eight times its size.

Kutúzov's expectation—that the surrender proposal (which committed him to nothing) would buy time for part of the transport to get through, and that Murat's mistake would soon be discovered—proved correct. As soon as Bonaparte, who was at Schönbrunn sixteen miles from Hollabrünn, received Murat's dispatch with the proposed truce and surrender terms, he saw through the ruse and wrote the following letter to Murat:
Schönbrunn, 25th Brumaire, 1805,
at eight o'clock in the morning
To PRINCE MURAT,

I cannot find words to express my displeasure. You command only my advance guard and have no right to arrange an armistice without my orders. You are costing me the fruits of a campaign. Break the armistice immediately and march on the enemy. Inform him that the general who signed that agreement had no authority to do so, and that no one but the Emperor of Russia has that right.

If, however, the Emperor of Russia ratifies that agreement, I will ratify it as well; but it is nothing more than a trick. March on, destroy the Russian army... You are in a position to seize its baggage and artillery.

The Russian Emperor's aide-de-camp is an impostor. Officers mean nothing when they have no authority; this one had none... The Austrians let themselves be fooled at the Vienna bridge crossing, and now you are letting yourself be fooled by an aide-de-camp of the Emperor.
NAPOLEON

Bonaparte's adjutant rode at full gallop with this furious letter to Murat. Bonaparte himself, not trusting his generals, moved out with the entire Guard toward the battlefield, determined not to let a ready victim escape. And Bagratión's four thousand men, meanwhile, cheerfully lit their campfires, dried and warmed themselves, and cooked porridge for the first time in three days—not one of them knowing or imagining what awaited them.
